title: Characterizing and Identifying the Prevalence of Web-Based Misinformation Relating to Medication for Opioid Use Disorder: Machine Learning Approach
screen_reason: Infodemiology study whose stated objective is to measure the prevalence of one specific, clinically discredited myth about medication for opioid use disorder ('agonist therapy is simply replacing one drug with another') across large opioid-keyword corpora from Twitter/X (6,365,245 posts), web-based health communities (Reddit 13,483,419 plus Drugs-Forum 5,549) and YouTube (99,386 comments), 1 January 2018 - 31 December 2019. A public-health expert annotated 800 semantically nearest posts, a supervised classifier (LR + TF-IDF, accuracy 0.91, AUC 0.9) was trained on those labels and applied to every post, and platform-level prevalences are reported: 0.9% Twitter, 0.58% YouTube, 0.4% web-based health communities. These are shares of items in a defined corpus judged against a clinical falsity standard, so CONTENT. The classifier is the instrument, not the contribution, so this is not excluded as detection/modelling work.

estimates.measure_type: % of opioid-keyword tweets classified as carrying the myth that medication for opioid use disorder is simply replacing one drug with another
estimates.value_raw: 0.9% for Twitter ('the prevalence of the stated MOUD myth ranged from 0.4% on web-based health communities to 0.9% on Twitter'; restated as '9 per 1000 posts on Twitter')
estimates.denominator: 6,365,245 tweets containing at least one of 152 curated opioid-related keywords, posted 1 January 2018 - 31 December 2019
estimates.definition: A post counted for the numerator if the trained classifier labelled it as relevant to the myth, i.e. as discussing MOUD and describing MOUD as using one drug to replace another
estimates.misinfo_def: "Health misinformation is defined as a health-related claim of a fact that is currently false because of a lack of scientific evidence"; the specific myth is "agonist therapy or medication-assisted treatment (MAT) is simply replacing one drug with another", which "has been discredited by evidence that MOUDs facilitate recovery"
estimates.source_quote: Specifically, the prevalence of the stated MOUD myth ranged from 0.4% on web-based health communities to 0.9% on Twitter.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results). Results, p. 4. The full Results sentence is 'The prevalence of posts among our sampled comments that were related to the myth that the use of MOUD does not constitute true recovery was 0.4%, 0.9%, and 0.58% for web-based health communities, Twitter, and YouTube, respectively.'; the two-column text rendering interleaves the columns line by line, so only single-line spans are contiguous. Restated in the Discussion, p. 9, as '9 per 1000 posts on Twitter'.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Supervised classifier (logistic regression on TF-IDF n-grams; accuracy 0.91, AUC 0.9, precision 0.85, recall 0.91, F1 0.88 in cross-validation) applied to all unannotated posts. Training labels came from public-health expert annotation of 800 posts (the 200 nearest neighbours per platform of the myth statement in an InferSent embedding space), within a 2,400-post annotation set covering several myths; 171 positive and 2,229 negative samples, rebalanced with SMOTE, 80/20 train-test split. Each myth's posts were annotated by the SAME single expert annotator for consistency, so no inter-annotator reliability is available.
estimates.moderator_quote: This resulted in a total of 152 keywords curated in the lexicon. ... For all the platforms we investigated, we focused on public posts and messages created between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2019. Our data set collection methodology for Twitter comprised querying for all tweets that included 1 of the words in our lexicon. This process yielded a total of 6,365,245 tweets.
estimates.notes: borderline=true for two reasons the adjudicator should weigh. (1) NUMERATOR IS ONE MYTH ONLY: the denominator is every opioid-keyword post but the numerator is a single discredited claim, so this is a strict lower bound on misinformation prevalence, not a general misinformation rate - the authors say so themselves ('at any time, there are likely multiple myths being discussed on the web, suggesting that the total volume of misinformation content related to opioids may be a substantial proportion of the total posts'). (2) STANCE NOT CODED: a stated limitation is that the study 'did not examine the nature of conversations surrounding the OUD treatment myth ... such as whether a conversation might be reinforcing or countering the myth', so posts rebutting the myth may sit in the numerator (the paraphrased Twitter example in Table 2 reads as a user arguing about, not endorsing, substitution). year set to 2019, the end of the two-year collection window (1 January 2018 - 31 December 2019).

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The three platform figures are reported only as percentages; numerators are never printed per platform. Table 3's footnote refers to '112,281 opioid-related posts identified by our best-performing model', which is consistent with the three percentages applied to their denominators (about 57,000 + 54,000 + 600), but it is not stated as a numerator breakdown, so no counts were entered as verbatim. 2) No pooled cross-platform prevalence is reported, so no pooled row exists; the three rows are on distinct, non-overlapping corpora and do not double-count each other. 3) Classifier metrics (accuracy 0.91, AUC 0.9, precision 0.85, recall 0.91, F1 0.88) and the top TF-IDF features are instrument properties, not estimates. 4) Pew figures quoted in Methods (18% of US adults use Reddit, 23% Twitter, 81% YouTube) are platform-use statistics cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8. 5) Judgement call for the adjudicator: whether a single-myth prevalence belongs in a general misinformation-prevalence pool at all. Numerator and denominator are radically asymmetric (one discredited claim vs all opioid-related posts), and the authors explicitly say total opioid misinformation 'may be a substantial proportion of the total posts'. If the review pools these values as 'misinformation prevalence', it will be pooling a lower bound of a different kind from the other content studies.

rob.design: Large-scale infodemiology / automated content analysis, CDC-funded. Frames: (a) Twitter - all public tweets containing any of 152 curated opioid keywords, 1 Jan 2018 - 31 Dec 2019, n = 6,365,245; (b) web-based health communities - 22 expert-selected opioid subreddits (1,189,590 posts + 12,293,829 comments) plus all 5,549 messages in the Drugs-Forum Opiates and Opioids subforums; (c) YouTube - all comments (99,386) on 552 videos whose titles contained one of 11 OUD-treatment keywords (keyword list restricted by API limits). Measurement: the myth statement was embedded with a bidirectional-LSTM InferSent encoder (4,096 dims), the 200 nearest neighbours per platform were pulled, and a single public-health expert annotated each of the 800 posts as relevant/not relevant to the myth (2,400 annotated posts overall across myths; 171 positive, 2,229 negative). SMOTE oversampling, 80/20 split, k-fold CV for LR/SVM and a held-out validation set for the LSTM; best model LR + TF-IDF (accuracy 0.91, AUC 0.9, precision 0.85, recall 0.91, F1 0.88), then applied to label every post. Key weaknesses: one annotator per myth so no inter-annotator reliability; classifier performance is estimated on a nearest-neighbour-enriched sample rather than a random sample of the corpus, so the error rate on the full corpus (where the positive class is 0.4-0.9%) is unknown and no confidence intervals or misclassification correction are given; stance (endorsing vs countering the myth) was not coded; only one of several known myths is measured; and, as the authors note, MOUD discussion occurs on many other platforms not covered.
rob.item6_quote: Health misinformation is defined as a health-related claim of a fact that is currently false because of a lack of scientific evidence [22]. ... In this study, we focus on one particular myth (and its language variants) related to MOUD: agonist therapy or medication-assisted treatment (MAT) is simply replacing one drug with another.
rob.item10_quote: The prevalence of posts among our sampled comments that were related to the myth that the use of MOUD does not constitute true recovery was 0.4%, 0.9%, and 0.58% for web-based health communities, Twitter, and YouTube, respectively.
